How the CSS trains

Every point gets six features: 1, x, y, x², y² and xy. The squared terms let the boundary curve into a circle, and xy lets it split four corners. The weights start at 0, and each epoch every point checks its score:

score = w·(45, 9x, 9y, x²−33, y²−33, xy) update = colour if colour × score ≤ $margin // wrong, or too close to the line w = w + Σ update × features / 15 // every point at once, all integers

Each line is a calc() over registered <integer> properties, written out $epochs times: $n_props properties that the browser recomputes on every click. The "≤" is a clamp(0, …, 1) step. The background is the model after the epoch you pick, scored again cell by cell. This is a perceptron, the 1958 ancestor of today's networks: one layer, trained the same way, with a margin.

The same rule runs in numpy in scripts/reference.py, and the test checks every weight of every epoch against it in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit. Digit recognizer · Source on GitHub.
